items.title: Macedonia and Philip II — The Springboard
items.body:
## Macedonia: Alexander's Home

- **Macedonia** was a kingdom **north of Greece** in the **Balkan Peninsula**, bordered by **Thrace, Epirus and Illyria**.
- Before Alexander it was a relatively **unknown kingdom**, overshadowed by powerful Greek city-states like **Athens and Sparta**.
- Under **King Philip II** (Alexander's father) Macedonia became the **dominant military and political power** in Greece.

## Philip II of Macedonia (r. 359–336 BCE)
- **Military reforms:** restructured the army, introducing the **phalanx** formation armed with long spears (**sarissa**), highly effective in battle.
- **Conquest of Greece:** subdued the Greek city-states after victory at the **Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE)**.
- Formed the **League of Corinth**, uniting most of Greece under **Macedonian hegemony**.
keyPoints: Macedonia lay north of Greece in the Balkans, bordered by Thrace, Epirus and Illyria.
Philip II (r. 359–336 BCE) turned Macedonia into Greece's dominant power.
He introduced the phalanx armed with the long sarissa spear.
Victory at the Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE) subdued the Greek city-states.
He formed the League of Corinth, uniting Greece under Macedonian hegemony.
items.mnemonic: Philip's toolkit — "PSCL": Phalanx, Sarissa, Chaeronea (338 BCE), League of Corinth.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Macedonia: The Home of Alexander; Philip II of Macedonia)

items.title: Alexander's Rise and the Road to India
items.body:
## Early Life and Accession

- Alexander was born in **356 BCE** in **Pella, Macedonia**, and was tutored by the philosopher **Aristotle** (philosophy, politics, science).
- In **336 BCE** Philip II was **assassinated**, and Alexander ascended the throne at the age of **20**, quickly eliminating rivals and securing the army's loyalty.

## From Persia towards India
- By **334 BCE** Alexander had **successfully conquered Persia**, and after defeating **Darius III of Persia** his ambitions led him further **eastward** toward the Indian subcontinent.
- **Reasons for the Indian campaign:**
  - The **riches and fertile lands of India** drew him after the defeat of Darius III.
  - **Reports of the wealth** of Indian kingdoms motivated deeper advance.
  - The Greeks already had **knowledge of India** through the **Persian Empire**, which held territories in present-day **Pakistan and Afghanistan**.
keyPoints: Alexander was born in 356 BCE at Pella and tutored by Aristotle.
He became king in 336 BCE (aged 20) after Philip II's assassination.
He conquered Persia by defeating Darius III, then turned eastward toward India.
Motives: India's riches and fertile lands, and reports of its wealth.
Greeks knew of India via the Persian Empire's holdings in modern Pakistan/Afghanistan.
Alexander decisively defeated Darius III of Persia at the Battle of Gaugamela (Arbela), 331 BCE, before advancing to India.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Alexander's Early Life and Rise to Power; Background & Reasons for Alexander's Indian Campaign)

items.title: Invasion Route & the North-West Kingdoms (327–325 BCE)
items.body:
## The Route into India (327 BCE – 325 BCE)

- Alexander's army crossed the **Hindu Kush** mountains into **Bactria** (modern Afghanistan) and continued into the **Indian subcontinent**.
- His forces passed through **Gandhara** (modern Pakistan) and advanced to invade the **Punjab** region of North India.

## The North-West Kingdoms
- Alexander faced **minor resistance** from local rulers such as **Ambhi, the King of Taxila**, who **submitted without a fight**.
- **Ambhi** became a **strategic ally**, providing Alexander with **troops and supplies** for his further campaigns.
- The strongest resistance lay further east, where **King Porus** ruled the land between the **Jhelum and Chenab** rivers.

figure.alt: Map of Alexander's invasion of the north-west c. 326 BCE showing his route through Bactra, Kamboja, Gandhara, Taxila, Puru (Porus), Bucephala and the retreat down the Indus to Patala
figure.caption: Alexander's invasion c. 326 BCE: the route through Gandhara and Taxila to Porus's kingdom on the Jhelum, and the return down the Indus.

keyPoints: Invasion of India spanned 327–325 BCE.
Route: Hindu Kush → Bactria → Gandhara → Punjab.
Ambhi, King of Taxila, submitted without a fight and became an ally.
Ambhi supplied Alexander with troops and provisions.
Porus, ruling between the Jhelum and Chenab, was the main resistance.
items.mnemonic: Route order — "HBG-P": Hindu Kush → Bactria → Gandhara → Punjab.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Alexander's Invasion of India 327–325 BCE — Invasion Route; Initial Campaigns — Ambhi of Taxila)

items.title: Porus and the Paurava Kingdom
items.body:
## King Porus

- The most significant Indian resistance came from **King Porus** (also known as **Purushottama**) of the **Paurava kingdom**.
- Porus ruled the region **between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers** in modern-day **Punjab**.
- The two armies met on the banks of the **Jhelum River (ancient Hydaspes)** in **326 BCE**.

## The Two Armies
- **Alexander** led a **seasoned, highly disciplined Macedonian army** of cavalry, infantry, archers and siege weapons.
- **Porus** commanded a **well-equipped Indian army** with a formidable **elephant corps**, crucial in Indian warfare.

figure.alt: Ancient Hellenistic-style mosaic depicting Alexander the Great charging into battle on horseback amid a clash of cavalry and spears
figure.caption: A Hellenistic depiction of Alexander in the thick of battle — the disciplined Macedonian cavalry that met Porus's elephant corps at the Hydaspes.

keyPoints: Porus (Purushottama) ruled the Paurava kingdom.
His territory lay between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers in Punjab.
The clash occurred on the Jhelum (ancient Hydaspes) in 326 BCE.
Alexander fielded disciplined cavalry, infantry, archers and siege weapons.
Porus relied on a formidable war-elephant corps.
items.mnemonic: Porus = Paurava, between two rivers — "J-C": Jhelum and Chenab.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Porus and the Battle of Hydaspes 326 BCE; The Battle of Hydaspes — Forces)

items.title: The Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE) — Strategy
items.body:
## The River in Flood

- The **Jhelum River** was in **full flood** during the battle, posing a significant **natural barrier**.
- Alexander used a **clever strategy** to cross undetected:
  - He **feigned movements** up and down the riverbank to confuse Porus.
  - He **secretly moved troops upstream at night** and crossed at an **unprotected spot** with part of his army.

## The Clash
- Porus deployed his **war elephants at the front**, hoping to intimidate the Macedonians.
- Alexander's soldiers **outflanked the elephants**, using **speed and discipline** to evade the massive animals.
- The Macedonian cavalry and infantry **harassed the elephants with javelins and arrows**, causing them to **panic and trample Porus's own troops**.
- Despite being **outnumbered**, Porus **fought bravely and led his army personally**, impressing Alexander with his valour.
keyPoints: The Jhelum was in full flood, a major natural barrier.
Alexander feigned movements, then crossed upstream at night at an unguarded point.
Porus massed his war elephants at the front to intimidate.
Macedonians outflanked the elephants and pelted them with javelins/arrows.
Panicked elephants trampled Porus's own troops; Porus fought on bravely in person.
items.mnemonic: Alexander's trick — "Feint, Night, Upstream": distract by day, cross by night, strike from upstream.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (The Battle of Hydaspes — Strategic Movements; The Battle; Porus' Resistance)

items.title: Outcome & the Treatment of Porus
items.body:
## Defeat and Capture

- Despite a brave fight, Porus's army was **defeated** by Alexander's **superior tactics** and well-trained forces, and **Porus himself was captured**.

## "Treat Me Like a King"
- Brought before Alexander and asked how he wished to be treated, Porus famously replied, **"Treat me like a king."**
- Impressed by his **courage and nobility**, Alexander **spared his life** and **restored his kingdom**.
- Porus was allowed to **retain his kingship** and was even given **additional territories** to govern as a **vassal** of Alexander.
- This reflects Alexander's broader approach: he often **respected brave local rulers** and let them keep power under his authority.
keyPoints: Porus was defeated by superior tactics and captured.
Asked how he wished to be treated, he replied 'Treat me like a king.'
Alexander spared his life and restored his kingdom.
Porus retained kingship and gained extra territory as Alexander's vassal.
Alexander typically respected and retained brave local rulers.
items.mnemonic: "Treat me like a king" — defeat → dignity → restored as a vassal king.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (The outcome of the Battle — Defeat of Porus; Aftermath and Treatment of Porus)

items.title: Significance of the Battle of Hydaspes
items.body:
## Why Hydaspes Mattered

- **Turning point:** one of the most important battles of Alexander's campaign, showcasing his **military brilliance** against a strong enemy with advanced tactics.
- **Costly victory:** though Alexander won, his army was **worn out** after years of campaigning and **reluctant to advance** further into India.
- **Elephants:** the battle revealed both the **power and limitations** of the **Elephant Corps**; the Macedonians, unfamiliar with elephants, devised effective **counter-tactics**.
- **Respect for Indian rulers:** Alexander's treatment of Porus exemplified his tendency to **respect brave leaders** and let them retain power under his authority.
keyPoints: Hydaspes was a turning point demonstrating Alexander's tactical genius.
It was a costly victory that left his army exhausted and unwilling to go on.
It exposed both the strength and the vulnerability of war elephants.
Macedonians improvised effective counter-tactics against elephants.
Alexander's respect for Porus modelled his approach to brave local rulers.
items.mnemonic: Hydaspes lessons — "TCE-R": Turning point, Costly win, Elephant limits, Respect for rulers.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Importance of the Battle of Hydaspes)

items.title: Mutiny at the Beas (Hyphasis) & the Retreat
items.body:
## The Turning Back

- After Hydaspes, Alexander advanced towards the **Beas River (the Greek Hyphasis)**, but his soldiers — **exhausted and fearful** of facing larger armies further east — **mutinied and refused to march further**.
- Reluctantly, Alexander **turned back** and **divided his forces**:
  - Part of the army **sailed down the Indus River**.
  - Alexander and the rest **marched through Gedrosia** (modern **Baluchistan**) back to Persia, suffering **heavy losses** in the harsh desert.
- Before leaving, Alexander **established Greek satrapies** (governorships) in the conquered territories to keep a **continued Greek presence**.

figure.alt: Map titled 'The Empire of Alexander the Great' showing his route from Macedonia across Persia to the Hydaspes (Jhelum) river in India, with battle sites and the extent of his empire
figure.caption: Alexander's empire and route — from Pella across Persia to the Hydaspes (Jhelum), the eastern limit of his advance before the Beas mutiny forced a return.

keyPoints: Alexander advanced to the Beas (Hyphasis) after Hydaspes.
His exhausted troops mutinied and refused to march further east.
He divided the army: part sailed down the Indus.
He marched back through Gedrosia (Baluchistan), losing many in the desert.
He left Greek satrapies to maintain a continued Greek presence.
His admiral Nearchus sailed the fleet from the mouth of the Indus to the Persian Gulf during the retreat.
items.mnemonic: End of the march — "Beas → Boats & Baluchistan": mutiny at Beas, one force by Indus boats, the other via Gedrosia (Baluchistan).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Alexander's Further Campaign in India — Advance, Retreat and Return; Establishment of Satrapies)

items.title: Death (323 BCE) & Fragmentation of the Empire
items.body:
## Death and Political Instability

- Alexander died in **323 BCE** (at Babylon) soon after returning from the Indian campaign — a widely established chronological anchor for the period.
- His **early departure** from India led to the **fragmentation of his empire**, with **local rulers reasserting control**.
- This **power vacuum** in the north-west paved the way for the rise of powerful Indian dynasties — above all the **Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya**.

> **Chronology anchor:** Alexander's Indian campaign (327–325 BCE) and death (323 BCE) provide one of the firmest **fixed dates** in early Indian history, helping anchor the chronology of the Mauryan rise that followed.
keyPoints: Alexander died in 323 BCE, shortly after leaving India.
His early departure fragmented the empire as local rulers reasserted control.
The north-western power vacuum enabled new Indian dynasties.
It notably paved the way for Chandragupta Maurya's Mauryan Empire.
The 327–325 BCE campaign and 323 BCE death are a key chronology anchor for early India.
items.mnemonic: "323 → Maurya": Alexander dies 323 BCE, the vacuum ushers in Chandragupta's Mauryas.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Impact — Political Instability, rise of the Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya); standard chronology for Alexander's death, 323 BCE

items.title: Impact of the Invasion on India
items.body:
## Lasting Effects

- **Spread of Hellenistic culture:** the invasion facilitated Hellenistic influence in the subcontinent, especially in **art, architecture and coinage**.
- **Foundation of cities:** Alexander founded cities such as **Alexandria on the Indus** and **Alexandria Bucephala** (named after his horse **Bucephalus**, who died after Hydaspes).
- **Greek influence on Indian culture:** the **Indo-Greek cultural exchange** had long-lasting impacts, especially in **North-West India**, influencing the later **Indo-Greek Kingdoms** (and, later, Gandhara art).
- **Trade & contact:** the campaign **opened land routes** and sustained **Indo-Greek contact** between India and the Hellenistic world.
- **Political consequence:** the empire's fragmentation cleared the path for the **Mauryan Empire**.
keyPoints: Spread Hellenistic influence in art, architecture and coinage.
Founded cities: Alexandria on the Indus and Alexandria Bucephala (after his horse Bucephalus).
Indo-Greek cultural exchange shaped North-West India and the later Indo-Greek Kingdoms.
Opened land trade routes and sustained Indo-Greek contact.
Fragmentation of the empire cleared the way for the Mauryan Empire.
items.mnemonic: Impacts "C-C-I-T-M": Culture (Hellenistic), Cities (Bucephala), Indo-Greek contact, Trade routes, Mauryan rise.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Impact of Alexander's Indian Campaign — Hellenistic culture, cities, Greek influence, political instability)
